segments.text: They were told Black men could not fight in tanks. The 761st Tank Battalion answered with 183 days of uninterrupted combat. They were the Black Panthers.
segments.image_title: SC 196107-S - Pvt. L.C. Byrd, Tuscaloosa, Ala., is a commander in a M-4 tank, near Nancy, France, 5 November 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain - U.S. Army Signal Corps

segments.text:
This is how they fought across Europe.

Activated in 1942, the battalion trained for nearly two years in the Jim Crow South — Kentucky, Louisiana, Texas.
segments.image_title: Parade of M-4 (General Sherman) and M-3 (General Grant) tanks in training maneuvers, Ft Knox

segments.text:
White units shipped overseas after two or three months. The 761st drilled, waited, and drilled again.

Then General George Patton came to review them. He said: "Men, you're the first Negro tankers to ever fight in the American Army.
segments.image_title: Lt. Gen. George S. Patton pins the Silver Star on Private Ernest A. Jenkins - NARA 535724

people.license_note: Commons: CC0 / Robert F. Cranston / Harry Warnecke

segments.text:
I would never have asked for you if you weren't good."

On November 7th, 1944, they entered the line in Lorraine, France, attached to the 26th Infantry Division — often at the very tip of the advance.
segments.image_title: SC 196105-S - M-4 medium tank in the mud near Nancy, France, 5 November 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain - U.S. Army Signal Corps

segments.text:
At Moyenvic, at Vic-sur-Seille, at Morville, the fighting was point-blank and brutal.

November alone cost them 156 casualties. Fourteen tanks were knocked out; twenty more were damaged.
segments.image_title: Knocked-out German and American tanks near Bezaumont, Meurthe-et-Moselle, France, 12 October 1944

segments.text:
They had been fighting for weeks. They would not be pulled from the line for months.

In December, the Germans smashed through the Ardennes. The 761st was rushed north to Belgium to relieve the surrounded 101st Airborne at Bastogne.
segments.image_title: M-4 Sherman Tanks Lined up in a Snow Covered Field, near St. Vith, Belgium

segments.text: At the town of Tillet, with just eleven tanks, they attacked for two straight days alongside the 87th Infantry Division. They lost nine tanks — and they took the town.
segments.image_title: SC 336804 - Tank destroyer going through belt of dragon's teeth, Siegfried Line
segments.license_note: Public domain - U.S. Army Signal Corps

segments.text:
After the Bulge, they smashed through the Siegfried Line itself, tearing open the road that let the 4th Armored Division pour into Germany.

Then came the drive across the Reich — town after town falling to the Black Panthers in an advance the Germans could not stop.
segments.image_title: SC 335254 - Tanks of the 9th Armored Division advance through Kleinbullesheim, Germany, 6 March 1945
segments.license_note: Public domain - U.S. Army Signal Corps

segments.text: On May 4th, 1945, alongside the 71st Infantry Division, they liberated the Gunskirchen concentration camp in Austria — freeing thousands of prisoners the Nazis had left to die.
segments.image_title: The Seventy-first Came - to Gunskirchen Lager (1945) - prisoners streaming from Gunskirchen, photo crop from scan page n5
segments.license_note: Public domain - U.S. Army, 71st Infantry Division unit history, published 1945; image is a crop of the booklet photograph

segments.text: Days later, at Steyr on the Enns River, they met troops of the Soviet Red Army — among the first Americans to do so. 183 days after it began, their war was over.
segments.image_title: ElbeDay1945 (NARA ww2-121) - 2nd Lt. William Robertson and Lt. Alexander Silvashko at the meeting of Soviet and American Armies, near Torgau

segments.text: The price was staggering: nearly half the battalion became casualties, and seventy-one tanks were lost. In return, they killed over six thousand German soldiers and captured nearly sixteen thousand more.
segments.image_title: M4 burning leipzig - SC 206454, M4 tank of Sgt. George K. Cuthbert Jr., Company C, 741st Tank Battalion
segments.license_note: Public domain - U.S. Army Signal Corps

segments.text: Sergeant Ruben Rivers refused to abandon his men after his tank was hit, fighting on until his wounds killed him. Fifty-three years later, America finally awarded him the Medal of Honor.
segments.image_title: SC 196106-S - Cpl. Carlton Chapman, machine gunner in an M4 tank, near Nancy, France, 5 November 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain - U.S. Army Signal Corps

people.image_title: File:Staff Sergeant Ruben Rivers, WWII Medal of Honor recipient (cropped).jpg

segments.text: They came home to prejudice, not parades. Thirty-three years later, in 1978, President Jimmy Carter presented the battalion with its Presidential Unit Citation. 183 days. Four campaigns. A continent crossed. Come out fighting.
